title: The hypertrophy series: the perfect progression scheme for muscle growth
summary: NH presents the two progression schemes he considers best for bodybuilders: linear progression, deliberately slowed using evolving references, and linear periodization driven by tonnage. He argues bodybuilders should not deload, keeping only small tonnage dips that are already built into evolving references.
claims: Progressive overload is the key and weight on the bar is its most reliable form
Linear progression is adding weight session to session without strategy, as in the novice honeymoon period
Easy novice linear progression spoils lifters; most quit when progress stops
Example of linear progression: 3x3 at 100 lb, next session 3x3 at 110 lb
Bodybuilders should deliberately slow linear progression to delay the big plateau, because time spent there still builds tonnage
Powerlifting pushes novices to become intermediates fast; bodybuilders want tonnage accumulation, not strength
Evolving references slow progression by making you repeat a weight for different rep ranges over several sessions, keeping you in relevant intensity windows
Static rep ranges are effectively linear progression, adding load every session
Novices should use evolving references early to build habits for linear periodization
Linear periodization means progressing less often by manipulating volume and intensity; bodybuilders should track tonnage progression
His programs already contain linear periodization through evolving references, even the novice ones in small doses
Intermediates struggle when they jump from low-volume novice programs into high-volume periodized programs
A deload is a big drop in volume, tonnage and intensity meant to produce a later increase
Bodybuilders shouldn't program deloads; with evolving references the dips are already built in
Ignore programs that only give a rep range like 6-10 without references; rep ranges should dictate progression
Bodybuilding progression should fluctuate less than powerlifting waves, with small planned tonnage-sacrifice periods
A week with fewer total reps at a higher weight is a tonnage sacrifice that sets up a later rise
Progression becomes a card game with volume, intensity and tonnage; sacrifice one to PR, then use the PR as a working weight to raise volume
Deloads are risky: coming back no stronger means you dipped for nothing; small dips are better long term
Seek sustainable progression, not progression at all costs
